html:
The Coast Salish are a large family of related peoples around the Salish Sea, the inland waters of Puget Sound and the straits of Georgia and Juan de Fuca, in today's British Columbia and Washington. They speak many related Salishan languages and were never one nation but dozens of independent villages and groups, such as the Duwamish, Suquamish, Musqueam, S'Klallam and Nisqually.

Salmon was the centre of life, caught with weirs, reef nets and traps, along with shellfish, camas roots and cedar for houses, canoes and clothing. Several families shared each long cedar plank house, and leaders gave away wealth at potlatch feasts. Weavers made blankets from mountain goat wool and the hair of a special breed of small woolly dog.

Smallpox swept the region in the late 1770s and 1780s, before most Europeans had even arrived. In the 1850s US treaties moved the Salish of Washington onto reservations, while in British Columbia small reserves were laid out without treaties. The city of Seattle is named after the Duwamish and Suquamish leader Si'ahl.
